Chaincode Upgrade and Versioning Strategies

Practical workflow and safety patterns to evolve your chaincode, perform schema migration, and keep ledger integrity.

Package → Install → Approve → Commit, then Init/Migrate when schema changes are required.

Non-idempotent migrations or wrong sequence break upgrades.

screens.title: Chaincode Lifecycle Explained
screens.narratorSegment: The chaincode lifecycle defines the coordinated steps organizations use to bring chaincode into operation on a channel. Package means bundling your source into a deployable artifact, typically a tarball with a label that identifies the version. Install places that package on endorsing peers so they have the code to execute transactions. Approve is an organization-level endorsement of a chaincode definition: each approving org submits metadata including the chaincode name, the human-readable version string, the required sequence integer, and any collection or endorsement policy configuration. Commit is the channel-level action that records a definition where enough organizations have approved it, making the new definition active on the channel. A key subtlety is sequence: the sequence number must be incremented for Fabric to treat the commit as a new iteration. Without raising the sequence, a commit will not replace the existing definition. This lifecycle enforces consensus and prevents unilateral upgrades. For example, packaging mychaincode_1.1 and installing it on peers does nothing until all required orgs approve and you commit with sequence incremented. Think of package and install as making the code available, approve as organizational consent, and commit as the channel agreeing on the new active version.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › Lifecycle Explained
Definition and Roles
Clear stages that control how code is made active on a channel.
Package
Create the chaincode tarball with a label that reflects your version.
Install
Place the package on endorsing peers so they can execute the code.
Approve
Each org records consent to the chaincode definition for the channel.
Commit
When enough orgs have approved, commit the definition to activate the new version.
Teaching Visual — Stage Cards
Practical note
  • Sequence must increase for Fabric to accept a new definition as an upgrade.
  • Version is a label for operators; sequence drives channel-level changes.
  • Install does not change channel state — approvals and commit do.
Example
peer lifecycle chaincode package mychaincode_1.1.tar.gz --path ./mychaincode --lang golang --label mychaincode_1.1
Key Takeaway
Treat sequence as the authoritative upgrade counter; always increment it for an upgrade.

screens.title: Packaging and Installing a New Chaincode
screens.narratorSegment: Packaging and installing are the steps that make new chaincode code available on your peers. Packaging produces a labeled artifact you can distribute to endorsing peers. The example package command creates a tarball with an explicit label that includes a version string; that label later helps you map the installed package to a package identifier. After packaging, install the package on each endorsing peer that should execute the chaincode. The peer install step prints a package identifier. Capture that package-id — it is required when you call approveformyorg. In practice you will automate packaging and parse the install output to retrieve the package-id reliably. A common pitfall is losing track of the package-id or using different labels across orgs, which breaks approval. For example, run peer lifecycle chaincode package mychaincode_1.1. tar. gz with a consistent label, then peer lifecycle chaincode install mychaincode_1.1. tar. gz on each peer. Keep the install output and package-id in your deployment notes so you can approve with the correct identifier. Packaging and Installing a New Chaincode means always record the package-id returned by install; approvals require that exact identifier.. In practical terms, concrete commands and the package-id you must capture. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › Packaging & Install
Commands to run
Package, then install on each endorsing peer and capture the package-id.
peer lifecycle chaincode package mychaincode_1.1.tar.gz --path ./mychaincode --lang golang --label mychaincode_1.1
peer lifecycle chaincode install mychaincode_1.1.tar.gz
# Save the package-id printed by the install command for approveformyorg
Why package-id matters
The package-id ties an installed binary to the chaincode definition approved by organizations; mismatched IDs prevent approvals from referencing the correct code.
Supporting Notes
  • Use identical labels across packaging and installation to reduce confusion.
  • Automate parsing the install output to avoid copy/paste mistakes.
  • Keep deployment metadata under version control alongside your chaincode.
Key Takeaway
Treat the package-id as essential deployment metadata required for approval.

screens.title: Approve and Commit — Version and Sequence Rules
screens.narratorSegment: Approve and commit turn installed code into an active chaincode definition on a channel. Each approving organization runs approveformyorg and provides parameters including the chaincode name, the package-id, the human version string, and a sequence integer. The channel accepts a commit only after enough organizations, per the lifecycle endorsement policy, have approved the same definition. The sequence integer is critical: it is a monotonic counter that must be incremented for every new definition committed. If you try to commit a definition with the same sequence as the channel already holds, Fabric treats it as the same iteration and will not effect an upgrade. In practice, if your previous commit used sequence 1, your upgrade should use sequence 2. The --init-required flag must be included in both approveformyorg and commit if the new chaincode version requires a one-time Init invocation. Commit commonly includes peerAddresses and tlsRootCertFiles so peers can endorse the commit transaction and waitForEvent to block until ordering and validation complete. A practical example shows how approveformyorg references the package-id and sets sequence and version together, so keep those values consistent across orgs.

keyIdea.text: Always increment sequence to signal a new chaincode iteration; pair it with a consistent version label and the package-id during approvals.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › Approve & Commit
Approve — Example
peer lifecycle chaincode approveformyorg -o orderer.example.com:7050 --channelID mychannel --name mychaincode --version 1.1 --package-id <package-id-from-install> --sequence 2 --init-required --waitForEvent
Note: include --init-required if your new code needs a one-time Init/Migrate call.
Commit — Example
peer lifecycle chaincode commit -o orderer.example.com:7050 --channelID mychannel --name mychaincode --version 1.1 --sequence 2 --init-required --peerAddresses peer0.org1.example.com:7051 --tlsRootCertFiles <org1_tls_root_cert> --waitForEvent
Commit requires enough endorsing orgs per the channel lifecycle policy to succeed.
Checklist
  • Confirm previous sequence and increment it for an upgrade.
  • Make sure all orgs approve the same package-id, version, and sequence.
  • Include --init-required consistently if Init must be invoked once after commit.

screens.title: --init-required and Init/Migrate Functions
screens.narratorSegment: The --init-required flag tells Fabric that the newly committed chaincode version exposes an Init or Migrate function that must run once after commit. This mechanism is useful when a schema change requires a coordinated migration step over the existing world state. If you declare --init-required during approve and commit, Fabric will reject ordinary transaction invokes until the special init invocation is performed. After commit, you must run peer chaincode invoke with --isInit to trigger the chaincode's Init function. The Init function should contain one-time setup or migration logic: for example, iterate existing assets and add a default value for a newly introduced field. A practical example is adding a CreationTimestamp field: the Init function can scan all assets, detect missing timestamps, and populate them with a derived or fixed value. Remember that Init is called only after the commit that included --init-required; failing to call Init leaves the chaincode in a state where normal application transactions may be blocked. Design the Init to be idempotent so retries or duplicate invocations do not corrupt state. --init-required and Init/Migrate Functions means use --init-required to enforce a single, explicit migration step after upgrade and make that step safe to re-run.. In practical terms, when and how to trigger one-time initialization after upgrade. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › Init / Migrate
Init Invocation Pattern
peer chaincode invoke -o orderer.example.com:7050 --channelID mychannel --name mychaincode --isInit -c '{"Args":["Init"]}' --peerAddresses peer0.org1.example.com:7051 --tlsRootCertFiles <org1_tls_root_cert>
The --isInit call triggers the chaincode's Init/Migrate logic exactly once in normal operation and unblocks normal transactions.
Design rules
  • Keep Init idempotent: detect existing migrations and skip updates if already applied.
  • Use transaction timestamps or fixed defaults when deriving new field values.
  • Log warnings for items that fail to migrate and continue safely.
Key Takeaway

--init-required plus a safe Init gives you a controlled migration step that can populate new schema fields across existing ledger data.

screens.title: How World State Handles Schema Changes
screens.narratorSegment: When you change the chaincode data model, existing world state entries remain unchanged until you migrate them. In Go, when json. Unmarshal reads stored JSON into a new struct that has additional fields, the new fields take their zero value if missing. For example, adding a CreationDate string to Asset means old assets read by GetState and unmarshaled into the new struct will get an empty string for CreationDate. This behavior is useful for additive, optional fields because code can accept a zero value and populate it lazily on first access or during a migration. More complex changes — such as renaming fields or splitting a field into two — require explicit migration logic. That is where Init or a Migrate function becomes essential: iterate over keys with GetStateByRange, parse values into a flexible map or intermediary structure, detect missing or renamed fields, construct the new representation, and PutState the updated JSON. Always code defensively: handle unmarshal errors, skip malformed entries with a warning, and ensure PutState failures are logged. Understanding this default unmarshal behavior helps you choose whether a full migration is necessary or whether a lazy population approach suffices.

keyIdea.title: Unmarshal Behavior
keyIdea.text: Adding optional fields is often backward compatible because missing fields become zero values on unmarshal, but structural changes may require explicit migration.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › Schema Evolution
Additive Fields

When the new struct adds a field, existing stored JSON without that field will unmarshal into the struct and set the new field to its zero value. This makes some upgrades safe without immediate migration.

Example
// old asset JSON: {"id":"A1","owner":"Bob","value":10}
// new struct adds CreationDate string; after unmarshal CreationDate == "" (zero value)
When to Migrate
  • Optional fields: consider lazy population or idempotent Init to fill defaults.
  • Renames or splits: require full migration to transform stored JSON to the new shape.
  • Always handle unmarshal errors and skip malformed entries with warnings during migration.
Tip

Use a flexible map[string]interface{} when reading old data in Init so you can adapt to multiple legacy shapes.

screens.title: Init/Migrate Example: Add CreationTimestamp
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the example Init function that migrates existing assets by adding a CreationTimestamp. The function begins by getting an iterator over all keys with GetStateByRange and handling errors. For each entry, the code unmarshals the stored bytes into a map so it can flexibly detect the presence of creationTimestamp. If the key lacks that field, the migration sets a default timestamp — in the example the current time formatted as RFC3339 — marshals the updated map back to JSON, and writes it with PutState. Critical practices in this code are idempotency and graceful error handling: the function checks for the field before adding it so repeated runs do not duplicate or corrupt data. It logs warnings on unmarshal or PutState failures and continues iterating. This pattern applies to many migration tasks: detect, transform, write, and keep the operation safe to re-run. When you implement similar logic, choose a reliable source for default values and ensure you handle partial failures so one bad record does not abort the whole migration unnecessarily. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › Init Code Example
Key excerpt (conceptual)
resultsIterator, err := ctx.GetStub().GetStateByRange("", "")
for resultsIterator.HasNext() {
    queryResponse, err := resultsIterator.Next()
    var assetMap map[string]interface{}
    err = json.Unmarshal(queryResponse.Value, &assetMap)
    if _, ok := assetMap["creationTimestamp"]; !ok {
        assetMap["creationTimestamp"] = time.Now().Format(time.RFC3339)
        updatedAssetBytes, _ := json.Marshal(assetMap)
        ctx.GetStub().PutState(queryResponse.Key, updatedAssetBytes)
    }
}
This shows the read-transform-write loop and the check that makes the migration idempotent.
Guidance
  • Use map unmarshalling to accept older shapes safely.
  • Log and skip malformed entries rather than failing the whole migration.
  • PutState in small batches if you expect many records to avoid long transactions.
Misconception

Don't assume PutState will always succeed for every key; plan for partial failures and retries.

screens.title: Lazy Population vs Full Migration
screens.narratorSegment: When adding a new field you have two common strategies: lazy population or a full one-time migration. Lazy population means you accept zero values when old assets are read and populate the new field on the first write or access. This is lightweight and avoids a large migration transaction, but it leaves older assets lacking the field until accessed and can produce inconsistent results if not carefully coded. Full migration uses an Init/Migrate that iterates over all items and populates the new field immediately for everyone. This gives consistent state at the cost of a possibly long-running operation and more complexity to handle failures or large datasets. Choose lazy population when the field is optional and correctness is not immediately required for all assets. Choose full migration when downstream logic depends on every asset having the new field or when searching/querying by the new field is required. In either case, design idempotent migration logic, test in staging under realistic dataset sizes, and consider a maintenance window for heavy migrations to avoid prolonged resource contention. Lazy Population vs Full Migration means use lazy population for optional fields and full migration when consistent, global state is required immediately.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Populate on first access or when creating new assets. Minimal immediate work and lower risk, but inconsistent until items are touched.

Full Migration

screens.title: Idempotency, Retries, and Safety Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Idempotency is the property that running the same operation multiple times produces the same result. For Init/Migrate this means detecting whether a record has already been migrated and skipping updates if so. This protects against transient failures where the Init transaction is resubmitted, or when commit transactions are replayed. To design idempotent migrations, check for the presence of the target field before writing, use version markers in state where appropriate, and write updates that are conditional rather than blind overwrites. Also plan for partial failures: log which keys failed and consider a retry mechanism outside the single Init transaction if you expect many problematic records. Keep transactions bounded and consider batching when migrating large datasets to avoid exhausting peer resources. Test failure scenarios in staging: simulate network drops, PutState failures, and replays. Finally, remember endorsement policy and ordering guarantees mean Init itself must satisfy the same lifecycle endorsement requirements and may be impacted by org-level policies during execution. Idempotency, Retries, and Safety Patterns means design init to be idempotent, handle partial failures gracefully, and test retries in staging under realistic failure modes.. screens.title: Common Upgrade Mistakes and Checklist
screens.narratorSegment: Operators frequently make a small set of recurring mistakes during upgrades that are straightforward to avoid with a checklist. First, failing to increment the sequence number is the most common error; Fabric will not treat the commit as an upgrade if the sequence is unchanged. Second, mismatching package-id values between installs and approve calls prevents approvals from referencing the correct installed package. Third, forgetting to include --init-required during both approveformyorg and commit when your chaincode requires Init leaves the chaincode blocked until you notice and invoke the init call. Fourth, writing non-idempotent Init logic can corrupt data when retrying failed transactions. Finally, skipping staging tests on realistic data volumes leads to unexpected performance or resource issues during large migrations. The checklist to avoid these mistakes is simple: record package-ids, confirm prior sequence and increment it, include --init-required when needed, write idempotent migration code, and run a full staging verification with pre- and post-upgrade queries. Keeping this checklist as a deployment playbook will reduce the likelihood of costly production incidents. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn why chaincode upgrades are a routine operational task and how Fabric's lifecycle supports safe, coordinated upgrades. We'll connect the lifecycle stages—package, install, approve, commit—with practical versioning and sequence rules that ensure channels adopt a new chaincode definition only when organizations agree. You will see a concrete upgrade scenario: moving an Asset chaincode from version 1.0 to 1.1, adding a new timestamp field, and using an Init or Migrate function to populate existing data. We'll also highlight common pitfalls—like forgetting to increment the sequence, skipping --init-required, or writing non-idempotent migration code—that can cause failed upgrades or data corruption. After this overview you'll understand when to perform a rolling upgrade versus scheduling a maintenance window, how the _lifecycle enforces consensus, and why test environments are essential. Think of this chapter as both a checklist and a practical walkthrough so you can upgrade with confidence and verify results.

By the end of these screens you'll be able to explain the chaincode lifecycle and perform an upgrade from packaging through commit. You will learn to run the peer lifecycle chaincode commands correctly, including packaging and installing a new chaincode label, and retrieving the package identifier required for approval. You will also identify when a schema change requires an Init or Migrate invocation and design an idempotent migration that populates new fields without corrupting existing data. Each objective ties to a demonstrated skill: packaging and installing, approving and committing with a proper sequence number, invoking Init when requested, and verifying post-upgrade state. These competencies let you upgrade chaincode with confidence and follow the operational checklist needed for safe production changes. Learning Objectives means you can perform a full upgrade flow and explain why sequence and --init-required matter.. In practical terms, skills you'll build and verify in this chapter. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

These supplemental objectives emphasize verification and operational detail. You will practice invoking the chaincode Init transaction after commit when --init-required is set, and learn how the Init function can be used as a migration entry point. You will also learn to increment the sequence number properly and understand how this numeric sequence differs from the human-readable version string. Finally, you'll be able to plan tests that query pre-upgrade assets, run the migration, and confirm the new field is present for both migrated and newly created assets. Together these objectives give you the habit of safe, repeatable upgrades that preserve ledger integrity. Learning Objectives (Continued) means verification is as important as performing the upgrade; plan queries and checks before and after migration.. In practical terms, practical verification and safety skills. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The chaincode lifecycle defines the coordinated steps organizations use to bring chaincode into operation on a channel. Package means bundling your source into a deployable artifact, typically a tarball with a label that identifies the version. Install places that package on endorsing peers so they have the code to execute transactions. Approve is an organization-level endorsement of a chaincode definition: each approving org submits metadata including the chaincode name, the human-readable version string, the required sequence integer, and any collection or endorsement policy configuration. Commit is the channel-level action that records a definition where enough organizations have approved it, making the new definition active on the channel. A key subtlety is sequence: the sequence number must be incremented for Fabric to treat the commit as a new iteration. Without raising the sequence, a commit will not replace the existing definition. This lifecycle enforces consensus and prevents unilateral upgrades. For example, packaging mychaincode_1.1 and installing it on peers does nothing until all required orgs approve and you commit with sequence incremented. Think of package and install as making the code available, approve as organizational consent, and commit as the channel agreeing on the new active version.

Packaging and installing are the steps that make new chaincode code available on your peers. Packaging produces a labeled artifact you can distribute to endorsing peers. The example package command creates a tarball with an explicit label that includes a version string; that label later helps you map the installed package to a package identifier. After packaging, install the package on each endorsing peer that should execute the chaincode. The peer install step prints a package identifier. Capture that package-id — it is required when you call approveformyorg. In practice you will automate packaging and parse the install output to retrieve the package-id reliably. A common pitfall is losing track of the package-id or using different labels across orgs, which breaks approval. For example, run peer lifecycle chaincode package mychaincode_1.1. tar. gz with a consistent label, then peer lifecycle chaincode install mychaincode_1.1. tar. gz on each peer. Keep the install output and package-id in your deployment notes so you can approve with the correct identifier. Packaging and Installing a New Chaincode means always record the package-id returned by install; approvals require that exact identifier.. In practical terms, concrete commands and the package-id you must capture. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Approve and commit turn installed code into an active chaincode definition on a channel. Each approving organization runs approveformyorg and provides parameters including the chaincode name, the package-id, the human version string, and a sequence integer. The channel accepts a commit only after enough organizations, per the lifecycle endorsement policy, have approved the same definition. The sequence integer is critical: it is a monotonic counter that must be incremented for every new definition committed. If you try to commit a definition with the same sequence as the channel already holds, Fabric treats it as the same iteration and will not effect an upgrade. In practice, if your previous commit used sequence 1, your upgrade should use sequence 2. The --init-required flag must be included in both approveformyorg and commit if the new chaincode version requires a one-time Init invocation. Commit commonly includes peerAddresses and tlsRootCertFiles so peers can endorse the commit transaction and waitForEvent to block until ordering and validation complete. A practical example shows how approveformyorg references the package-id and sets sequence and version together, so keep those values consistent across orgs.

The --init-required flag tells Fabric that the newly committed chaincode version exposes an Init or Migrate function that must run once after commit. This mechanism is useful when a schema change requires a coordinated migration step over the existing world state. If you declare --init-required during approve and commit, Fabric will reject ordinary transaction invokes until the special init invocation is performed. After commit, you must run peer chaincode invoke with --isInit to trigger the chaincode's Init function. The Init function should contain one-time setup or migration logic: for example, iterate existing assets and add a default value for a newly introduced field. A practical example is adding a CreationTimestamp field: the Init function can scan all assets, detect missing timestamps, and populate them with a derived or fixed value. Remember that Init is called only after the commit that included --init-required; failing to call Init leaves the chaincode in a state where normal application transactions may be blocked. Design the Init to be idempotent so retries or duplicate invocations do not corrupt state. --init-required and Init/Migrate Functions means use --init-required to enforce a single, explicit migration step after upgrade and make that step safe to re-run.. In practical terms, when and how to trigger one-time initialization after upgrade. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When you change the chaincode data model, existing world state entries remain unchanged until you migrate them. In Go, when json. Unmarshal reads stored JSON into a new struct that has additional fields, the new fields take their zero value if missing. For example, adding a CreationDate string to Asset means old assets read by GetState and unmarshaled into the new struct will get an empty string for CreationDate. When adding a new field you have two common strategies: lazy population or a full one-time migration. Lazy population means you accept zero values when old assets are read and populate the new field on the first write or access. This is lightweight and avoids a large migration transaction, but it leaves older assets lacking the field until accessed and can produce inconsistent results if not carefully coded. Full migration uses an Init/Migrate that iterates over all items and populates the new field immediately for everyone. This gives consistent state at the cost of a possibly long-running operation and more complexity to handle failures or large datasets. Choose lazy population when the field is optional and correctness is not immediately required for all assets. Choose full migration when downstream logic depends on every asset having the new field or when searching/querying by the new field is required. In either case, design idempotent migration logic, test in staging under realistic dataset sizes, and consider a maintenance window for heavy migrations to avoid prolonged resource contention. Idempotency is the property that running the same operation multiple times produces the same result. For Init/Migrate this means detecting whether a record has already been migrated and skipping updates if so. This protects against transient failures where the Init transaction is resubmitted, or when commit transactions are replayed. To design idempotent migrations, check for the presence of the target field before writing, use version markers in state where appropriate, and write updates that are conditional rather than blind overwrites. Also plan for partial failures: log which keys failed and consider a retry mechanism outside the single Init transaction if you expect many problematic records. Keep transactions bounded and consider batching when migrating large datasets to avoid exhausting peer resources. Test failure scenarios in staging: simulate network drops, PutState failures, and replays. Operators frequently make a small set of recurring mistakes during upgrades that are straightforward to avoid with a checklist. First, failing to increment the sequence number is the most common error; Fabric will not treat the commit as an upgrade if the sequence is unchanged. Second, mismatching package-id values between installs and approve calls prevents approvals from referencing the correct installed package. Third, forgetting to include --init-required during both approveformyorg and commit when your chaincode requires Init leaves the chaincode blocked until you notice and invoke the init call. Fourth, writing non-idempotent Init logic can corrupt data when retrying failed transactions. Finally, skipping staging tests on realistic data volumes leads to unexpected performance or resource issues during large migrations. The checklist to avoid these mistakes is simple: record package-ids, confirm prior sequence and increment it, include --init-required when needed, write idempotent migration code, and run a full staging verification with pre- and post-upgrade queries. Keeping this checklist as a deployment playbook will reduce the likelihood of costly production incidents.
